questions.q: What does the Central Limit Theorem state about the sampling distribution of the sample mean $\bar{x}$?
choices: When sample size $n$ is sufficiently large ($n \geq 30$), the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is approximately normal, regardless of the population shape
As $n$ increases, the population becomes normally distributed
The sample standard deviation approaches the population standard deviation
Every random sample will have an identical mean
questions.answer: The CLT states that for sufficiently large $n$ (conventionally $n \geq 30$), the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ approaches normality even if the underlying population is skewed or non-normal.

questions.q: If a population is already normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$, what is the shape of the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ for a small sample of $n = 5$?
questions.answer: When the original population is normally distributed, the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$ is normal for any sample size $n$.

questions.q: Does the Central Limit Theorem apply to the shape of the individual sample data values?
choices: No, it applies only to the distribution of sample statistics across repeated sampling, not the sample data itself
Yes, individual observations become normal as $n$ grows
Only if the data has no outliers
Yes, this is known as the Law of Large Numbers
questions.answer: The CLT describes the sampling distribution of the statistic $\bar{x}$, never the distribution of individual data points in a single sample.

sections.heading: Section 2: Mean and Standard Error of the Sample Mean

questions.q: A population has mean $\mu = 80$ and standard deviation $\sigma = 20$. For random samples of size $n = 25$, what are the mean and standard error of $\bar{x}$?
To cut the standard error of the sample mean $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ in half, the sample size must be:
questions.answer: Because $n$ is under the square root in the denominator, multiplying $n$ by $4$ divides the standard error by $\sqrt{4} = 2$.

questions.q: When using the formula $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$, what condition must be satisfied if sampling without replacement?
choices: The $10\%$ condition: sample size $n \leq 0.10 N$ (population size)
questions.answer: The $10\%$ condition ($n \leq 0.10 N$) ensures that sampling without replacement is close enough to independent that the standard error formula remains valid.

sections.heading: Section 3: Sampling Distribution of Sample Proportion p-hat

questions.q: In a large population, $40\%$ of adults support a referendum ($p = 0.40$). For random samples of $n = 100$, what are the mean and standard deviation of $\hat{p}$?
Which conditions justify modeling the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ with a normal distribution?
questions.answer: The Large Counts Condition requires both expected successes $np \geq 10$ and expected failures $n(1 - p) \geq 10$.

questions.q: Why is the sample proportion $\hat{p}$ called an unbiased estimator of $p$?
choices: The mean of its sampling distribution equals the true population parameter $p$
It never makes a prediction error
It is computed from a simple random sample
questions.answer: An estimator is unbiased when the expected value (mean of its sampling distribution) equals the true population parameter being estimated.

questions.q: A tire manufacturer knows tire lifespan is normal with $\mu = 50000\text{ miles}$ and $\sigma = 4000\text{ miles}$. What is the probability that an SRS of $16$ tires has a mean lifespan under $48000\text{ miles}$?
How does increasing sample size affect the bias and variability of a sample statistic?
choices: Variability decreases, while bias remains unchanged
questions.answer: Increasing sample size reduces sampling variability (standard error narrows), but has no effect on bias (which stems from study design).

questions.q: If $X_1$ and $X_2$ are independent sample means from two populations, what is the standard error of $(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2)$?
questions.answer: Variances of independent sample means add: $\sigma_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = \sqrt{\sigma_{\bar{x}_1}^2 + \sigma_{\bar{x}_2}^2} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}$.
